chunks: Realistic resistor model and parasitics. The question: Draw a realistic circuit model for a resistor. What are the parasitics and where do they come from?
An ideal resistor has only resistance.
A real one also has a little inductance (a tendency to resist quick changes in current), because current through its leads and body makes a magnetic field.
It also has a little capacitance between its two ends, which lets fast signals leak across.
The standard model is the resistance R in series with a small inductance, with a small capacitance across the whole thing. At low frequency only R matters.
At high frequency the extras take over.
Imagine a toll booth on a road. The booth is the resistance. A heavy revolving door at the booth resists quick changes in traffic, like the inductance.
A side road runs around the booth, like the capacitance. At slow speeds, traffic uses the booth. At high speeds, cars take the side road and never meet the booth.
The analogy is loose, but it shows the idea of a path that only fast signals take.
R and L s carry the DC and low-frequency current; C p sits across both and provides the high-frequency bypass. The dashed box is the physical package, whose terminals are 1 and 2.
Series inductance ( L s ): the small inductance of the leads and body. It matters most for low-value resistors.
Parallel capacitance ( C p ): the small capacitance across the two terminals. It matters most for high-value resistors.
Corner frequency: the frequency where the extra part starts to change the impedance noticeably.
Impedance: the total opposition to an AC (back-and-forth) signal, in ohms, including these extras. Parasitic: an unwanted hidden property.
Take a 10 kilohms chip resistor with 0. 1 picofarads across it.
The capacitance lets signals sneak around the resistor above f equals 1 over (2 pi R C p) , which is about 160 megahertz. Below that, it acts like 10 kilohms.
Now take a 10 ohms resistor with 1 nanohenries in series. Its inductive corner is R over (2 pi L s) , about 1. 6 gigahertz. That is the whole idea.
"A real resistor is the ideal R in series with a small inductance, from the leads and the current path, with a small capacitance across the whole thing from the terminations.
High-value resistors go capacitive first: 10 k with 0. 1 picofarads has a corner near 160 megahertz. Low values go inductive.
The best behaved is near the square root of L over C, roughly 80 ohms for a chip. Wirewound parts are the worst because they're coils."
